newsitem.title: UK: Physical aluminium picks up, premiums stable.
newsitem.headline: Physical aluminium picks up, premiums stable.

text.p: Falling futures prices and some increased offtake for the final quarter has injected a modicum of interest into Europe's physical aluminium market, although there has been little real change in premiums, traders said.
Continued light availability of off-grade metal Meanwhile meant that discounts for the Russian A6, A5, and A0 were again being shaved, although the tightness was not particularly acute.
"Generally I would say the market is stabilising at present and there are bits and pieces of business going on," one trader said.
"There has been a little bit more demand in September than in August," another trader said.
On the London Metal Exchange (LME), three months prices have fallen sharply recently, and on Monday were trading at $1,427 a tonne -- the lowest level for two years.
Traders said that the decline from levels above $1,500 at the start of the month has generated some consumer interest, but this is patchy at best as the market could well fall further.
"The market will be in oversupply in early 1997, with demand growth running at one percent this year, while supply is perhaps three percent," another trader noted.

However, although there was plenty of metal available in Europe, it was in locations such as the UK and Scandanavia, not on the Continent where consumers will need it. This would help to maintain premiums to some extent, he added.

Total LME inventory stood at 947,700 tonnes with some 583,000 tonnes in the UK's warehouses and around 195,000 tonnes in the two Swedish delivery locations. In Rotterdam meanwhile the total was 119,175 tonnes.

Western ingots in Rotterdam have traded recently in the $20/25 range over LME, while Russian A7E, also LME-deliverable, has been trading around $20. In the off-grades, Russian A6 continued to be indicated around level to a small discount with business at LME flat.

Traders said there was less off-grade metal this year as many of the Russian smelters have improved their production methods and increased quality. Similarly, many manufacturers were opting for the off-grades to reduce unit costs.
There may be little downside to the overall premium/discount structure, as the market was in a full contango of $34.50/35.00, which encouraged people to hold and finance metal, they said.
Elsewhere, there were reports of slightly softer premiums in the Far East, with cif Japan 1997 trading at $55, against previous levels in excess of $60.
In the U.S., Midwest premiums were said to be stable around the $3.50/lb level.
